Tuesday
Our class is running the no-plastic campaign, and I got to write the slogan. I spent all of maths on it. Final version: "Bag it, don't bin it!" I was so proud. Short, rhymes, fits on a badge.
Then Irfan read it at break and said, "Wait, bag what? Put the plastic in a bag?"
I said no, bring a cloth bag, don't throw plastic in the bin.
He said, "The little kids will think it means put plastic in a bag and keep it."
I wanted to argue. But then I asked my cousin in Class 3, and she said exactly what Irfan said.
So now it's "Carry cloth, not plastic." Less clever. But the Class 3 kids get it, and they're the ones who throw most of the wrappers.
Five words can mean five things, depending on who's reading.
- Arohi

qa.q: What was Arohi's first slogan?
qa.a: "Bag it, don't bin it!"

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when Irfan questioned the slogan?
qa.a: Arohi felt proud of the slogan and a bit defensive, wanting to argue, before checking and accepting the point.

qa.q: What small step helped Arohi fix the slogan?
qa.a: Testing it on a Class 3 cousin, the actual audience, showed how younger children would read it.

qa.q: How might the Class 3 students read the first slogan?
qa.a: They might take it literally as putting plastic into a bag and keeping it, missing the message about cloth bags.

grounding: The diary shows a teenager writing a campaign slogan whose compressed meaning is read differently by a different audience.

In the village of Kothur, Ira and Shalini were writing a skit for the Gram Sabha on saving water. Their first script ended with a big line: "Men waste, women carry!"
They practised it at the well. Shalini's uncle heard and frowned. "So all of us are wasters now?" Two other men walked off.
Ira was annoyed. "But it's true in our lane! Who fetches water every morning?"
Shalini thought for a while. "True, but if half the audience walks out, who hears the rest?"
They sat on the well's edge and rewrote it. The new last scene showed a father and a daughter both carrying pots, then fixing a leaking tap together. The last line became: "Every drop, every hand."
At the Gram Sabha, the men clapped. Afterwards Shalini's uncle came up and asked where he could get the tap washers.

qa.q: What was the first script's big line?
qa.a: "Men waste, women carry!"

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when the men walked off?
qa.a: Ira felt annoyed and frustrated, because the line reflected something real in their lane.

qa.q: Which choice of the girls worked, and why?
qa.a: Rewriting the ending to show everyone sharing the work kept the message but let the whole audience hear it without feeling attacked.

qa.q: How did Shalini's uncle read the first line?
qa.a: He read it as an insult to all men, calling them wasters, which made him stop listening.

grounding: The scene shows teenagers writing a skit script whose short line compresses an attitude that different audiences read differently.

passage:
In the small town of Bhor, the Sunday cricket match ended with Siddharth run out on the last ball. His team lost by one run.
That evening Ojas texted him: "nice job genius"
Siddharth stared at it. He was already feeling terrible. Was Ojas mocking him? He typed, "Thanks for rubbing it in," and threw the phone on the bed.
Ojas saw the reply and frowned. He'd meant it as a joke between them, the way they always teased. But without his grin and his voice, it looked cruel.
He didn't type another message. He called.
"Siddharth, I was joking. Badly. I know you feel bad. That run-out could've happened to anyone. The umpire was blind anyway."
There was a pause, then a small laugh on the line.
"Next time," Siddharth said, "add a laughing face or something."
"Or just call. Calls are better."

qa.q: How many runs did Siddharth's team lose by?
qa.a: His team lost by one run.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he read "nice job genius"?
qa.a: Siddharth felt hurt and humiliated, already upset about the run-out, and read the text as mocking.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that fixed the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Instead of texting again, he called, explained it was a bad joke, and acknowledged Siddharth's feelings.

qa.q: How did Ojas see his own message at first?
qa.a: He meant it as their usual friendly teasing and only realised from the reply that, without his grin and voice, it looked cruel.

grounding: The scene shows a joking message read as rude without face or voice, and a phone call clearing it up.

It was late in Toronto when Nadia typed to Bilal: "lol I think we're moving to Calgary."
She added the "lol" because she didn't know how else to say it. She'd been crying for an hour.
Bilal replied fast: "haha sure, and I'm moving to the moon 🚀"
Nadia's throat tightened. She put the phone face down and didn't answer.
Bilal waited. Nothing. Usually she'd send a joke back. He scrolled up, read her message again. The "lol" looked strange now. Why would she joke about that?
He typed, "wait. are you serious?" Then deleted it and called.
"Nadia? Sorry. I thought you were joking. Are you actually moving?"
She was quiet, then said, "Yeah. Dad's job. In June."
"That's huge. I'm really sorry I laughed."
They stayed on the phone for an hour.

qa.q: Where was Nadia's family moving?
qa.a: To Calgary.

qa.q: Why did Nadia add "lol" to her message?
qa.a: Nadia felt sad and unsure how to say something so big, so the "lol" softened it, even though she'd been crying.

qa.q: What could Nadia and Bilal try next time a message feels unclear?
qa.a: Add a clarifying line, like "I'm serious," or call, as Bilal did, instead of guessing the tone.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt when he realised she was serious?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and embarrassed for laughing, and wanted to make it right, which is why he called.

grounding: The scene shows a serious message read as a joke because of a "lol," and a call clarifying the real feeling.

Binita had just become secretary of the school's eco club. On Monday she posted in the club group: "Meeting at 5. Be on time. Bring your notebooks."
Within minutes, Himani messaged her privately. "Um, are you angry with everyone?"
Binita was confused. "No? Why?"
"It sounds like a teacher telling us off. Short sentences. Full stops. Some of the juniors think they're in trouble."
Binita read it again. In her head it had sounded efficient. On the screen, with no smile, it looked stern.
She added a second message: "Hi all! Just to be clear, nobody's in trouble 🙂 Excited for our first meeting. See you at 5, and bring notebooks for ideas."
Three juniors sent hearts within a minute.
At the meeting, a Class 8 boy said, "I thought you were going to scold us."
"Me too, apparently," Binita laughed.

Chandrika uploaded her first song cover on a Friday night: a slow old Hindi song, recorded on her phone in the bathroom for the echo. She sent the link to the class group.
Hearts came quickly. Thumbs-up. A few fire emojis. By midnight, thirty reactions.
But not from Ujjwal. Her best friend since Class 2.
She checked at one. At seven. At ten. Nothing. Was he embarrassed for her? Did he hate it?
By Saturday afternoon she'd convinced herself he thought it was terrible.
Then at four, a message: "CHANDRIKA. Just got network at Nani's village. Listened three times on the bus stand. The second verse!!! 🤍"
She laughed out loud in the kitchen. Her mother looked over.
"Nothing," Chandrika said, grinning. "Just a very late heart."
She wrote in her notes app: no reaction is not a reaction.

qa.a: By midnight, thirty reactions.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling while waiting for Ujjwal's reaction?
qa.a: Chandrika felt anxious and hurt, reading the missing reaction as a sign he thought the song was terrible.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt reading Chandrika's worry, if she told him?

Last year, when my friend Eshaan's grandfather was in hospital, he stopped talking much at school. He'd post one line on his status some nights: "long day." "tired."
I didn't know what to say. So I just reacted with a heart every time. Sometimes a folded-hands one. I worried that it was too small, that he'd think I was lazy.
Months later he told me the hearts helped. "I didn't want to talk. But I'd see yours and know someone saw it."
It went the other way too. After his grandfather got better, Eshaan stopped reacting to my posts for weeks. I started wondering if I'd done something wrong. Then I remembered the hearts. Sometimes you're just busy living.
I asked him once, lightly. He said, "Sorry, I've just been off my phone."
Small signals matter. Missing ones usually don't.
- Tanuja

qa.a: Tanuja reacted with a heart every time, sometimes a folded-hands one.

qa.a: Tanuja was anxious that the hearts were too small and that Eshaan would think it was lazy support.

qa.a: Sending quiet hearts worked, because Eshaan didn't want to talk but still felt seen, and later asking lightly cleared up the missing reactions.

I'm Pradeep, and I'm in the class group where it happened. Tarun, Neeraj and I have been friends since Class 5, and we have one GIF we always use: a cartoon cow slowly falling off a cliff. It means "well, that went badly." Everyone in our trio laughs.
On Monday a new student, Farah, posted that she'd failed the first maths test. Tarun replied with the cow GIF.
I laughed. Then I saw Farah had gone offline straight away.
I don't know what she thought. Maybe she thought Tarun was laughing at her.
I messaged Tarun: "She doesn't know the cow."
He went quiet, then wrote to her privately: "Sorry, that GIF is our 'I failed too' thing. I got 12 in that test. Want to study together?"
She replied with a laughing face and "ok, show me the cow."

Saturday: Seema and her cousin Lakshmi texted almost only in GIFs. A dancing grandmother for good news. A crying cat for tiring days. It was their private language.
Wednesday: Lakshmi messaged: "didn't get the dance school place." Seema was on the bus and quickly sent their crying-laughing cat, meaning "nooo, ugh." Lakshmi didn't reply. Then, an hour later: "wow ok. thanks."
Seema's stomach sank. Without their usual jokes around it, the laughing cat looked like she was laughing at the rejection.
She called straight away. "Lakshmi, I'm so sorry. I meant 'nooo', not 'haha'. That's awful news."
"It felt like you thought it was funny."
"I don't. At all."
Next Saturday: They agreed on a rule. GIFs for fun stuff. Words, or a call, for big stuff. Lakshmi sent a GIF of the cat with a bandage. Seema sent a heart.

Manoj, you think your class group invented reaction GIFs? Sit, let your Asif Chacha tell you.
When I was sixteen, our class had one favourite: a clip of an old film hero falling off a horse. We used it for everything. Failed test? Horse. Rained on sports day? Horse.
Then a new boy, Ravi, joined. First week, he posted in the group that his cycle had been stolen. I sent the horse. Meant it as "oh no, bad luck."
He didn't come to school the next day. When he came back, he wouldn't look at me.
My mother said, "Did you ever tell him what the horse means?"
I hadn't. So I did. Walked to his house and explained it, and said sorry.
He laughed, a little. "I thought everyone was laughing at me."
We were friends for twenty years after that. He still sends me the horse.

qa.a: Ravi likely felt hurt and humiliated, thinking the whole class was laughing at his loss.

qa.a: His mother's question, which led Asif to walk to Ravi's house, explain the in-joke and apologise.

passage:
Sunday
Scrolled through Pranav's holiday photos again. Beach sunset. Mango ice cream. His whole family laughing on a boat. Perfect filters. And I was stuck at home with fever all week.
I'll be honest, diary: I felt resentful. Why does he get a perfect life?
Then today at the library he said, "That trip was the worst. My parents fought the whole time. The boat photo was the only five minutes they were smiling."
I didn't know what to say. I just said, "I'm sorry."
It made me think about my own posts. I only post when my hair's good and the light's nice. Nobody sees me with fever and a tissue box.
So I posted a photo of me today, blanket and all. Caption: "real life 🤒." Then I asked Mehr before posting the one with her in it too.
- Zeenat

qa.a: He said the boat photo was the only five minutes they were smiling.

qa.a: Zeenat felt resentful and a bit envious, comparing a week of fever to what looked like his perfect holiday.

qa.q: What changed in how Zeenat chooses what to post?
qa.a: Zeenat posted an honest, unfiltered photo and asked Mehr's permission before sharing one with Mehr in it.

qa.a: He might feel lonely or strange, since the posts hide how hard the trip really was.

passage:
When I invited Akash to my birthday lunch, his reply was just: "okay."
With a full stop. No emoji. I spent the whole evening decoding it. In my friend group, "okay." with a full stop means you're annoyed. Like, "fine, whatever."
Next day I asked him carefully, "Are you upset about something? Your okay seemed cold."
He looked totally lost. "Cold? I always use full stops. My dad's an English teacher. He'd die if I didn't."
I laughed so hard. I scrolled up our chat. He'd written "okay." to literally everything, including "I got you a samosa."
So now I know: my group reads a full stop as cold. His family reads no full stop as lazy. Same dot, two meanings.
He came to the lunch. He brought a card. It said: "Happy birthday. See you soon." Full stops everywhere.
- Kiran

qa.q: What was Akash's reply to the invitation?
qa.a: Just "okay." with a full stop.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while decoding the reply?
qa.a: Kiran felt anxious and hurt, worrying that the full stop meant Akash was annoyed.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that cleared up the confusion?
qa.a: Kiran asked Akash directly and gently instead of assuming, which revealed the full stop was just his habit.

qa.q: How does Akash's family see full stops compared with Kiran's friends?
qa.a: Akash's family sees them as correct and polite, while Kiran's friend group reads them as cold.

grounding: The account shows a full stop being read as cold in one group and normal in another, so punctuation suggests but does not prove a mood.

Counsellor's note - Kashish, Class 9, Monday
Nirmala came to see me at break, upset. She said her mother had been angry with her all weekend. When I asked why she thought so, she showed me the texts: "COME HOME BY 6." "DID YOU EAT?" "CALL ME WHEN YOU REACH."
All in capitals. Nirmala said, "She's shouting at me in every message."
I asked if her mother had sounded angry on the phone. Nirmala thought and said, "No. Normal. She asked about my test."
We looked at the messages again together. No harsh words, only capital letters. I wondered aloud if her mother simply types that way, perhaps with caps lock on, or because it's easier to read.
Nirmala laughed for the first time. "She does hold the phone very far away."
She agreed to ask her mother that evening. Tuesday she told me: caps lock, stuck for a year.

qa.q: What did one of the mother's texts say?
qa.a: "COME HOME BY 6."

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she came to see Kashish?
qa.a: Nirmala felt upset and anxious, believing her mother was shouting at her in every message.

qa.q: How did Kashish help Nirmala read the messages differently?
qa.a: Kashish asked how her mother sounded on the phone and looked at the words with her, suggesting other reasons for capitals before assuming anger.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's mother feel if she learned her caps looked like shouting?
qa.a: She would probably feel surprised and sorry, since she was only checking on her daughter.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows capital letters read as shouting, and the reader learning such cues suggest but don't prove a mood.

Asif sent me this after I told him about the science fair: "OKAY!!! that is sooooo cool"
First I was thrilled. Then I started wondering. OKAY with three exclamation marks. Is he shouting? Is "sooooo" sarcastic? My brother says long vowels mean someone's making fun of you.
But Asif doesn't really do sarcasm. And he'd been asking about the project all week. And his last message had a party emoji.
So maybe it was just... excitement.
I didn't want to guess forever, so I texted: "haha was that real excitement or sarcastic excitement?"
He replied: "REAL. why would I be sarcastic?? can I come see it?"
My brother reads it one way, Asif writes it another. I'm learning to look at the person, not just the letters.
- Indu

In their village near Bishnupur, the drama troupe practised every evening in the school courtyard. Bidisha had the role of a daughter who shouts at her father for selling the family's land.
For three weeks she spoke the lines flatly. Shankar Kaka, the director, finally stopped her. "Don't read it. Feel it. When were you last angry and couldn't say anything?"
Bidisha thought of something. She didn't say what. The next time, her voice cracked with fury, and she threw the prop bundle of papers on the ground. The courtyard went silent.
Afterwards she sat on the step, shaking but lighter.
A neighbour aunty came over. "Is that happening in your house, Bidisha?"
"No, Kaki. It's a play," Bidisha said calmly. "I just used a feeling."
Shankar Kaka nodded at the aunty. "That's acting. We borrow feelings, not stories."

In an after-school improvisation class in Busan, the teacher called out: "Two friends at a train station. One is leaving forever. Go."
Soo-ah stepped in. Gabriel played the friend staying behind. At first it was funny. Then Soo-ah went quiet. She picked up an invisible suitcase, put it down, picked it up again. Her hand hovered near Gabriel's shoulder and didn't land.
"Write to me," Gabriel improvised, and his voice shook a little too.
When the scene ended, the class clapped slowly.
Afterwards Gabriel asked, "Was that you? Leaving?"
Soo-ah shook her head. "My cousin moved to Canada last month. I never got to say goodbye properly. This was... a goodbye I could practise."
The teacher, overhearing, said gently, "That's what improv is for. If you ever want to talk about your cousin, not in a scene, I'm here."

qa.a: To Canada, last month.

qa.a: It suggested she was feeling a real sadness about goodbyes, hesitant and grieving, even inside the role.
